books.section: Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, B. The Cultures of African-American Communities

primary_sources: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845

stimulus.text:
This daguerreotype portrait of Frederick Douglass, made by Samuel J. Miller in 1847–1852, shows Douglass from the chest up, dressed as a respectable gentleman in a dark coat, white shirt, and bow tie, staring straight at the viewer with a stern expression.

"You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man." — Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845, on his fight with the overseer Edward Covey in August 1833.
stimulus.source_note: Portrait viewed before writing: Samuel J. Miller, daguerreotype of Frederick Douglass, 1847-1852, Art Institute of Chicago. Quotation verbatim from Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, Miller daguerreotype of Douglass, 1847-1852, public domain
stem: In the Covey passage, “how a slave was made a man” refers to Douglass

options.text: learning to read in secret as a boy
options.misconception: That is the reading story; this passage is about the fight with Covey.

options.text: buying his freedom from Thomas Auld
options.misconception: Douglass escaped in 1838; his freedom was bought later by English friends.

options.text: resisting Covey’s beating and refusing to be broken
leaving Maryland for New York in 1838
options.misconception: The fight happened in August 1833, five years before the escape.

rationales.A: Reading matters in the Narrative, but this passage is about Covey. The manhood here comes from the fight.
rationales.B: Douglass did not buy his freedom from Auld. He escaped in 1838, and English friends later bought his freedom.
rationales.C: Covey made a man into a slave by breaking him. Douglass fought him for two hours and was never whipped again.
rationales.D: The escape came in 1838. The fight with Covey came first, in August 1833.
rationales.general:
1. Follow the sentence. Covey made a man into a slave by breaking him; Douglass reverses it.
2. Find the turning point. Douglass fights Covey for two hours and is never whipped again.
3. Name the meaning. Manhood means refusing to be broken.
Background: Douglass was sixteen when Thomas Auld rented him out to Covey, a man known as a slave-breaker.
Remember: when a writer flips a sentence, follow the flip.
